Images for computer vision

Source: vignettes/images.Rmd
images.Rmd

Classifying camera trap images with machine learning requires balanced datasets of representative images for each known species. WildObs records the species in every image of an observation, so its openly hosted images come labelled. This vignette finds those images, joins them to their labels, and downloads a small batch. It uses a 2023 University of Queensland teaching survey at Dwyers Scrub Conservation Park, Queensland, where a curated selection of images is hosted by the Tagged Image Repository of WildObs and the Atlas of Living Australia (ALA).

# load the R package 
library(WildObsR)

# your personal API key, read from .Renviron (see the Get started vignette)
api_key <- Sys.getenv("WILDOBSR_API_KEY")

# specify the project to access 
id <- "QLD_Dwyers_Scrub_ANIM3018_2023_WildObsID_0005"
# download the data package, while including the media resource, and take the first value in the list
dp <- wildobs_dp_download(api_key = api_key, project_ids = id, media = TRUE)[[id]]
# extract the media table from the data package 
media <- frictionless::read_resource(dp, "media")

Which images can be downloaded

Most WildObs images stay with the people who collected them. However, WildObs curates a selection of images from openly shared projects based on the number of detections within a project (e.g., species with few detections retain all images, while species with many detections retain an image per detection). Only images with filePublic = TRUE are openly hosted by WildObs or the ALA, and only those can be downloaded. The rest are listed, with their timestamps and labels, but their filePath reads not_publicly_accessible, and file names are withheld from public users.

# inspect how many images in this project are hosted openly
table(media$filePublic)
#> 
#> FALSE  TRUE 
#> 13208  8302

Across the whole public database the share of openly hosted images is small, so check filePublic before planning a training set.

Label each image with its species

Each media row carries the observationID it belongs to, a WildObs addition to Camtrap DP. Joining on it gives every image the species, count and observation type recorded for that observation:

# extract the observations table, read with their schema types
obs <- frictionless::read_resource(dp, "observations")
# specify the label columns of each observation
labels <- obs[, c("observationID", "observationType", "scientificName", "count")]

# merge the relevant observation fields to each public image with its label
public <- merge(media[media$filePublic, c("mediaID", "deploymentID", "observationID",
                                          "timestamp", "filePath")],
                labels, by = "observationID")

# view the species with the most openly hosted images
head(sort(table(public$scientificName[public$observationType == "animal"]),
          decreasing = TRUE), 8)
#> 
#>         Alectura lathami    Notamacropus dorsalis Notamacropus rufogriseus 
#>                     3450                      889                      832 
#>  Leucosarcia melanoleuca         Wallabia bicolor        Isoodon macrourus 
#>                      538                      361                      169 
#>             Macropodidae         Perameles nasuta 
#>                      163                      159

Subset to the species you need straight away. A project’s openly hosted images may occasionally include records that do not belong in a training set, such as misidentified blanks or images of people, and working with one species keeps them out. Here, the Australian brush-turkey (Alectura lathami):

# the openly hosted images of brush-turkeys only
turkey <- public[public$observationType == "animal" &
                   public$scientificName %in% "Alectura lathami", ]
# how many images do we have?
nrow(turkey)
#> [1] 3450

Projects also differ in whether they host blank images (observationType == "blank"). This one does; keep some in a training set, because models must also learn to say that nothing is there.

Download a batch

The function wildobs_media_download() saves each file into a folder per project and deployment, skips files already on disk, and reports what happened to each one. Start with a few files to check the setup before downloading thousands:

# start with six brush-turkey images, as a test batch
batch <- utils::head(turkey, 6)

# specify the folder where the images will be saved (temporary directory)
out_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "wildobs_images")
# and download them into that folder
result <- wildobs_media_download(batch, out_dir = out_dir)
#> 6 of 6 media files have a path that can be tried (6 web, 0 Google Cloud, 0 on this computer).
#> downloaded: 6

# check what happened to each file, and where it went
table(result$downloadStatus)
#> 
#> downloaded 
#>          6
# what are the file names of the images saved to your computer
basename(result$localPath)
#> [1] "T1_C1_Sclero_Z_Amir_mediaID_1.jpg" "T1_C1_Sclero_Z_Amir_mediaID_4.jpg"
#> [3] "T1_C1_Sclero_Z_Amir_mediaID_5.jpg" "T1_C1_Sclero_Z_Amir_mediaID_2.jpg"
#> [5] "T1_C1_Sclero_Z_Amir_mediaID_3.jpg" "T1_C1_Sclero_Z_Amir_mediaID_8.jpg"

The returned table keeps every column you passed in, so the labels stay with the files: result$scientificName names the species in each result$localPath. Write it out with the images, for example as labels.csv, and the batch is ready for training.

Cite and credit

Images are licensed with their project by a Creative Commons licence that requires attribution. Check the media licence, and cite the project in any model or dataset you publish:

# the licence that applies to this project's images
extract_metadata(dp, "licenses")[, c("name", "scope", "path")]
#>        name scope                                         path
#> 1 CC-BY-4.0  data https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/
#> 2 CC-BY-4.0 media https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

# and the reference to cite
writeLines(cite_datapackages(dp))
#> Zachary Amir & Annabel Smith (2023). WildObs Camera Trap Data Package: UQ's undergraduate widlife techonologies camera trapping module comparing human and AI comptuer vision [Camera Trap Data Package]. WildObs National Wildlife Camera Database. https://wildobs.org.au. RAiD: https://raid.org/10.83062/a3efd562. WildObs data package version 1.1.0.
